video.title: They Banned My $35K/Month Page So I Started a Business

summary: Chris Koerner launches Plans of Grandeur by selling his existing creator training materials to his newsletter subscribers after Facebook bans his page. He tests $47 and $97 one-time prices, then uses several email and payment-link tests to refine the offer and checkout. He reports building the business around existing videos, spreadsheets and documents, with most delivery moving into a School community. The central takeaway is to use an existing audience and useful material, launch quickly, and test price and messaging with small, randomized groups before emailing the rest of the list.

speakers.name: Chris Koerner
speakers.description: The Koerner Office host and solo presenter.

ideas.name: Plans of Grandeur creator training
ideas.one_liner: Sell a growing library of creator training materials and AMAs as a one-time digital product with a community.
ideas.business_model: One-time purchase for lifetime access to digital training, with recorded AMAs and new content added over time.
ideas.customer: People who want to grow a personal or business brand, make content or go viral, including faceless creators.
ideas.problem: They want practical help creating content, growing an audience and building a brand, but need training and examples.
ideas.offer: Existing videos, spreadsheets, guides and documents from Chris's Google Drive, later organized into School folders. Buyers also receive 12 AMAs, recordings of those AMAs and future creator training content.

pricing.model: One-time lifetime payment; the initial launch tested two prices and Chris later chose $97.
pricing.notes: The presale email described a 67% discount from the planned full price. Chris later chose $97 and tested email copy, price visibility and Stripe versus School checkout.

acquisition_channels.details: Chris segmented and randomized active newsletter subscribers, then sent identical emails with different prices and payment links to test the offer. He later emailed the rest of the list.

quote.text: I'm going to take a sample of my entire email list and launch not just like test, but launch the business with a Stripe link to pay
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

acquisition_channels.details: Chris documented the launch in a YouTube video, referred viewers to the offer and asked them to share it with potential customers.

quote.text: If you know anyone that might want to start doing content either for themselves or for their business, faceless or with their face, AI generated or not, please share this with them
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

ideas.delivery: Digital materials were initially hosted in Google Drive. Chris's business partner downloaded and organized them into folders in a School community. Stripe payment links could redirect buyers to the content; Chris says he had set up automatic invites or additions to School after Stripe payment. AMAs were to be recorded and added to the program.
unit_economics_claims: Chris says the content had already been created and that the business was almost pure profit, with Stripe transaction fees as the only stated cost.
He reports 111 transactions at about $80 per transaction and $8,300 revenue during an early update.
He reports generating $30,000 to $40,000 net profit over the course of the video, including A/B test emails.
ideas.startup_cost: Not stated. Chris says the materials already existed; the only ongoing cost he names is Stripe's 3% transaction fee. He separately bought a domain for $11.28 per year.
ideas.time_to_first_revenue: Chris says the first $97 payment arrived in under two hours from the idea.

acquisition.how: Newsletter segmentation and campaign sending can be automated after a person has subscribed. The initial offer, audience selection and tests still need human decisions. UK email marketing rules require the right consent for individual subscribers.

onboarding.how: Stripe payment links and the stated automatic School invite or add flow can handle routine onboarding, with occasional checks for failed payments or access problems.

delivery.how: The core offer is recorded digital material delivered through Google Drive or School, so software can provide access without routine manual work.

billing.how: Stripe takes one-time payments and can redirect buyers after checkout. Refund decisions and payment issues may still need a person.

support.how: The materials are self-serve, but Chris promised live AMAs and notes that customers can generate support requests, complaints and refund requests.

uk_applicability.notes: A digital training library and paid online community can be sold in the UK. The channel shown is an existing newsletter audience; UK rules on marketing email still apply, especially for individual subscribers.

risks: The original revenue stream depended heavily on Facebook, which Chris says banned his page without reinstating it.
A digital product must deliver the value promised; Chris says poor value relative to sales promises gives courses a bad reputation.
A founder with a small or nonexistent audience may not reproduce results from Chris's established newsletter.
A one-time lifetime offer combined with future content and AMAs creates an ongoing obligation to maintain the library and serve buyers.

ideas.name: Facebook creator content monetization
ideas.one_liner: Publish creator content on Facebook and earn income from a large following and related monetization.
ideas.business_model: Not fully stated; Chris describes making monthly income on Facebook and using his follower audience as data for profitable ads.
ideas.customer: Not stated. The platform audience is viewers of Chris's creator content.
ideas.offer: Creator videos and Facebook content; Chris refers to a video about how he makes money on Facebook.

pricing.model: Platform monetization and advertising-related income; exact mechanism not stated.
pricing.notes: Chris does not explain which Facebook monetization products generated the income.

acquisition_channels.details: Chris posted creator videos to Facebook; one video was also posted to Facebook and he says the page was banned hours later.

quote.text: And it had to have been because of that video because I also posted that video to Facebook. Hours later, banned
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

ideas.delivery: Chris published content on Facebook. He says he had a large content team and that Facebook followers were useful as data points for running ads. Exact content production and monetization processes are not stated.
unit_economics_claims: Chris says a video described making $35,000 per month on Facebook.
He says his page generated hundreds of thousands of dollars a year before the income disappeared after the ban.
He says the business had real costs, including a content team, so it was not 100% profit.
ideas.startup_cost: Not stated. Chris says he had a large content team and real business costs but gives no amount.

acquisition.how: Content publishing and distribution can use software, but planning, creation and audience development still need substantial human work. Paid ads require monitoring.

onboarding.how: No customer onboarding process is described; the audience relationship and platform access depend on the account and content team.

delivery.how: Content is digital, but Chris describes a large content team producing it. The account's removal also stopped delivery through Facebook.

billing.how: Platform monetization may be processed by Facebook, but the transcript does not describe billing or payout operations.

support.how: Chris describes extensive calls and correspondence with Meta support after the ban, with no automated resolution.

uk_applicability.notes: Creator content can be produced in the UK, but the model depends on platform rules, monetization eligibility and an audience. Chris's stated results and platform access are not shown to transfer directly.

risks: A platform can remove a page and income abruptly; Chris says his account was banned and not reinstated.
The transcript describes a copyright or intellectual property infringement claim that Chris disputes.
The content team creates costs, so platform revenue is not all profit.
Paid advertising effectiveness may depend on follower data and platform access.

ideas.name: Newsletter publishing and monetization

ideas.business_model: Newsletter audience monetized through paid offers; Chris points to courses and events as possible products.
ideas.customer: Newsletter readers interested in the creator's subject matter.
ideas.offer: Regular newsletter content and paid offers to subscribers. Chris also recommends a newsletter as an asset for selling a business offer.

pricing.model: Not stated for the newsletter itself; possible revenue from paid products, courses and events.
pricing.notes: The transcript gives third-party income examples and general advice, but no newsletter subscription price.

ideas.delivery: Chris writes and sends email through Beehiiv. He says the founder of Beehiiv sends one email per week, but does not describe subscriber acquisition for that example.
unit_economics_claims: Chris says the Beehiiv founder earns $500,000 a year from a list smaller than his and sends one email per week.
Chris says a newsletter with 2,000 subscribers could make tens of thousands of dollars or more a year from events and high-ticket courses.
ideas.startup_cost: Not stated. Chris says he has posted free beginner-level tutorials on starting a newsletter with little money.

acquisition.how: Newsletter publishing software can automate signup flows and campaigns, but audience growth methods are not described.

onboarding.how: Subscription confirmation and welcome flows can be handled by newsletter software; Chris says he chose not to send a welcome email when tagging existing subscribers.

delivery.how: Email campaigns can be scheduled and sent by software, although a person still needs to create useful content.

billing.how: No paid newsletter billing process is described; monetization is through offers rather than a stated paid subscription.

support.how: Reader replies and issues would likely need human attention; the transcript gives no support process.

uk_applicability.notes: Newsletter publishing and selling digital offers work in the UK. UK marketing rules apply to email campaigns, particularly messages to individuals and sole traders.

risks: The revenue example about Beehiiv's founder is second-hand and has no supporting operating detail.
Newsletter monetization depends on having an engaged list and an offer that readers value.
Email marketing to UK individuals requires appropriate consent.

tactics.name: Start from an unfair advantage
steps: List audience access, work history, skills and experiences that give you insight into a market.
Choose an offer that uses one of those existing advantages.
For Chris, that was a newsletter he could sell to.

quote.text: anytime anyone starts a business, you need to go to your unfair advantage. Everyone has an unfair advantage.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

tactics.name: Launch a minimum offer before polishing the brand
steps: Choose a workable name and move forward without hiring a branding agency or conducting a friend survey.
Create a payment link and write the first sales email.
Aim to get a first customer quickly so real sales data can guide improvements.

quote.text: I just want to launch. I want revenue. That's what I preach, right? You guys have heard me say that. Get your first customer as soon as possible.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

tactics.name: Randomize subscribers before an email price test
steps: Export active subscribers and paste them into a spreadsheet.
Use a random number formula, sort by that value, and remove the formula column.
Split a small sample into groups so older or more loyal subscribers do not skew one test group.
Use separate tags or segments for each price group.

quote.text: I want to perfectly randomize this list because what I'm about to do is what's called an AB test or a split test.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

tactics.name: Test prices with identical email copy
steps: Send the same subject line and email copy to equal-sized audience samples.
Change only the payment link and price between the groups.
Compare sales and revenue per subscriber, then allow time for higher-priced buyers to decide.
Refund buyers if a later test establishes that they paid more than the final test price.

quote.text: If I send both of those identical emails, it's the same email, same subject, same wording, same everything. The only thing that's different is the payment link with the price
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

tactics.name: Reduce checkout friction
steps: Ask only for information needed to complete the purchase.
Do not add fields such as names or phone numbers if the seller already has the information or does not need it.
Test whether an external community checkout adds account-creation friction compared with a Stripe payment link.

quote.text: The more friction you add to the checkout process, the more your conversion rate will drop. I don't care what it is you're selling. Do not add friction.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

tactics.name: Show the price before the click
steps: Test short emails with the price stated near the link against emails where the price is hidden until checkout.
Use separate payment links to track each variant.
In Chris's test, the version that disclosed the price performed better, so he chose to state the price in the full-list email.

quote.text: So the lesson, tell them the price in the email. That's what we're going to do here.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

tactics.name: Track each checkout link separately
steps: Create separate Stripe payment links for each test.
Use Stripe payment-link analytics to compare results when the price is the same but the checkout destination or email copy differs.
Exclude people who already received a test email from later sends.

quote.text: If we want to see how many people are using each of the payment links, we go into the payment link in question and then we click payments and analytics.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

tactics.name: Repurpose existing material into a paid library
steps: Inventory existing training videos, guides, documents and tracking spreadsheets.
Package useful material as an initial paid offer.
Organize the files into a cleaner course or community interface after validating demand.

quote.text: we basically downloaded all of the Google Drive content and uploaded it here uh into separate folders.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

tactics.name: Use a repeatable digital fulfillment flow
steps: Take payment through a Stripe link.
Redirect buyers to the hosted content or automatically invite them into the community.
Use a short welcome video and clear folders to orient new members.
Record live AMAs so people who miss them can still access the material.

quote.text: I can still automatically invite or add them to school after they pay on Stripe. I already have the automation set up.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

tactics.name: Stand behind the value of a course
steps: Make a clear promise about what the buyer gets.
Ensure the product provides the promised value.
Use the material to help buyers take action rather than selling unsupported outcomes.

quote.text: They only have a bad rap because so many of them don't match the value that the salesperson promises.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

evidence_quality.rationale: Chris demonstrates the setup and shares first-hand sales, email and payment-link results across several updates. The process is relatively specific, but the transcript contains inconsistent or garbled figures, the results are not independently verified, and his established audience makes the launch difficult to generalize.
evidence_quality.promotional_conflict: Chris sells Plans of Grandeur in the video and promotes it to viewers. He also speaks favorably about Beehiiv and says he links beginner tutorials, but no sponsor relationship is disclosed.
